name: Kingdom of Norway (medieval)
summary: The Norwegian kingdom united after Harald Fairhair (about 872); at its height under Haakon IV it ruled Iceland and Greenland, then joined Denmark and Sweden in the Kalmar Union (1397).

location.value: Western Scandinavia and the North Atlantic.

terrain.value: Mountains and high plateaus, with deep fjords and many islands along a very long Atlantic coast.

climate.value: Cold winters inland; the coast is milder and wet thanks to the Gulf Stream.

resources.value: Fish, especially stockfish (dried cod from Lofoten), timber, furs, iron, and walrus ivory from Greenland.

disasters.value: The Black Death reached Bergen in 1349 and killed perhaps half the population.

population.value: Perhaps about 300,000–500,000 people before the Black Death, falling sharply after 1349.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Norse settlement of the Atlantic islands.

economicBase.value: Farming and herding, fishing, and the export of stockfish, timber and furs.

tradeRoutes.value: Stockfish was traded through Bergen, where German Hanseatic merchants dominated trade from the 1300s.

wealth.value: Modest; the crown and the church held much land, and Bergen grew rich on the fish trade.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver pennies were minted from around 1000; kings collected land rents, fines and taxes from farmers.

inequality.value: Kings, nobles and church owned much land, while many farmers were tenants; thralls existed until about 1200.

governmentType.value: A Christian monarchy, with power shared with nobles and the church and limited by regional assemblies.

keyRulers.value: Harald Fairhair. Olaf II (St Olaf). Haakon IV.

succession.value: Disputed among royal sons until laws of the 1160s and 1260s fixed the crown to one legitimate heir.

institutions.value: Regional assemblies (things) and Magnus VI’s national law code (Landslov) of 1274.

stability.value: The civil wars ended in 1217 with the appointment of Håkon IV Håkonsson, who set clear succession laws.

eliteConflict.value: Rival claimants and factions such as the Birkebeiner and Baglers fought for the throne in the civil war era.

armyAndTech.value: Leidang levy fleets of longships and later cogs, with infantry and armoured noble retainers.

majorWars.value: Battle of Stiklestad (1030); Battle of Largs (1263).

territoryChange.value: Iceland and Greenland accepted Norwegian rule (1261–64); the Hebrides and Man were lost to Scotland in 1266.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals and partners included Denmark, Sweden and Scotland; England was a major trading partner.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Norwegian shipbuilding and stave-church carpentry were highly skilled.

scienceEducation.value: Church and cathedral schools; the King’s Mirror (about 1250) taught science and conduct.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Coastal shipping along the “north way”, mountain paths, and skis and sledges in winter.

religion.value: Christianity, accepted from about 1030; the archdiocese of Nidaros (Trondheim) was founded in 1152–53.

languageWriting.value: Old Norse, written in runes and then the Latin alphabet; laws and sagas were written down.

artsArchitecture.value: Stave churches such as Urnes, Nidaros Cathedral and Haakon’s Hall in Bergen.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles (lendmenn), clergy, free farmers and fishermen, tenants and, early on, thralls.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king, the church and St Olaf, alongside strong regional identities.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Denmark, Sweden, Scotland, England and the Norse settlements of the Atlantic islands.

ideasReligions.value: The cult of St Olaf at Nidaros, a major pilgrimage centre for Scandinavia.

colonisation.value: Norse settlement of Iceland, the Faroes, Orkney, Shetland and Greenland, later ruled by the Norwegian crown.

riseSignals.value: According to tradition, Harald Fairhair unified Norway in 872.

peakPeriod.value: Under Haakon IV (1217–63) Norway reached its greatest extent and cultural flowering.

declineSignals.value: The Black Death in 1349 killed many people, and royal unions with Sweden and Denmark followed.

outcome.value: Olaf IV inherited the Norwegian and Danish thrones in 1380; the Kalmar Union formed in 1397; the constitution was adopted on 17 May 1814 and the union with Sweden ran from 4 November 1814 until 7 June 1905.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
